stories.title: Twelve killed and 300 injured in Riyadh airport attack
stories.summary: At least 12 people were killed and 309 others injured in a strike on Riyadh's international airport, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation officials said, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to vow a decisive response against Yemen's Houthis. The coalition blamed the Iran-backed group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a "full-fledged war crime" that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile. The attack came during an unprecedented wave of Houthi strikes on the kingdom since a truce in the group's long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July. Four Saudi citizens were among the dead, as well as two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. Admissions by Saudi authorities of strikes hitting civilian targets are relatively rare, and aviation officials did not mention the Houthis by name. Operations were suspended at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport following the attack, the Saudi civil aviation authority said earlier.

stories.title: Is next Wednesday's public sector strike now inevitable?
stories.summary: The money is there and both sides say they want to do a deal so how are we facing into a massively disruptive public sector strike on Wednesday? More than 300,000 workers including nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants will engage in a 24-hour work stoppage and take to the picket lines. It will lead to the closure of schools, the cancellation of hospital appointments and massive disruption to public services. Unions are threatening another strike a week later on 21 October. So how did it come to this? In the early hours of the morning of 26 January 2024, following overnight talks, bleary-eyed trade union negotiators and Government officials emerged from the Workplace Relations Commission to announce that a new public sector pay deal had been agreed. It provided for pay increases of 10.25% and over a two-and-a-half-year period.

stories.title: Govt wants to honour RTÉ funding agreement - Taoiseach
stories.summary: The funding was expected to reach €260 million for 2027 as part of a €725m three-year agreement but instead will stand at €240m - representing a decrease of €20m. Mr O'Donovan said the decrease was due to his dissatisfaction with what he called the broadcaster's progress in implementing promised reforms. In an email to staff on Wednesday, Mr Bakhurst said that the decision "is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact on our ability to deliver our five-year strategy". Mr Bakhurst attended a meeting with Mr O'Donovan yesterday, and he described the outcome of those talks as "extremely constructive". "I’m not going into specifics and timelines. I mean, just I can tell you, 48 hours before Budget, there was a lot of issues that I was dealing with in terms of both expenditure and on social protection. Those were the bigger issues that I was focused on in terms of specific areas around cost of disability payment." Asked whether Mr O’Donovan had gone on a "solo run", the Taoiseach said he would not characterise it in that way and he said the estimates was a tough process for everybody.
stories.rssSummary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said that the Government wants to honour the funding agreement made with RTÉ and he said he believed the issue can be resolved.

stories.title: High Berth Rate: The growth of the cruise industry
stories.summary: Last week Dublin Port welcomed Atlas Ocean Voyages' World Voyager, which was wrapping up a ten-night cruise from Reykjavik. The ship’s arrival also happened to mark the end of Dublin’s 2026 cruise ship season. Meanwhile the Port of Cork will welcome three cruise liners in the coming days – bringing its season to an end. Cruises have become an increasingly important part of the Port of Cork’s business – with the regular arrival of ships, and their thousands of passengers, estimated to contribute more than €17m to the local economy. But cruises have become an increasingly significant part of the global tourism industry as a whole. According to Cruise Lines International Association, there were 37.2 million passengers on ocean-going cruise ships last year. That’s a more-than 25% increase on the numbers that travelled pre-pandemic, in 2019.
stories.rssSummary: Despite some bad press in recent months, the cruise industry continues to grow rapidly - while profits at the biggest players outstrip anything their landed industry-mates could dream of, writes Adam Maguire.

stories.title: Will the American death row system change after Pike?
stories.summary: More than 1,600 men and women have been executed in the United States since the 1970s. And while executions have declined significantly over the past 20 years, the fierce debate surrounding them was reignited this month following a botched execution and the US president's approval of another execution by firing squad. Death row inmate Christa Pike, who murdered another woman when she was 18, was set to become the first woman in 200 years to be executed in Tennessee, until a shocking series of events. She survived two doses of a lethal injection and her botched execution has been described as "torture" by her lawyers and the "worst" incident the NGO 'Death Penalty Information Center' has seen. Attempts to stop the execution, citing her age at the time of the crime and her mental health history, were denied. So too was a request to explore an alternative to lethal injection, with her lawyers arguing that her small veins and other medical conditions left her afraid that something would go wrong. Christa Pike is now conscious in hospital, with swollen arms and an inability to swallow, according to her legal team.

stories.summary: A locality from where the local GAA club, Shamrock Gaels, draws some of its base. Pressing matters this week are Sunday's senior county final at Markievicz Park, where the 'townies' St Mary's are the opposition. Gaels are the defending champions, looking to win the Owen B Hunt for just the fourth time. The mention of Riverstown, population 394, as of the 2022 census, also provides a link to the now infamous Lansdowne Road riots and, more satisfyingly, to that joyous evening for Ireland in the Puskas Arena last November. The Kenny name resonates well beyond the idyllic village and the trickling River Arrow. Johnny Snr cut a dash for Sligo Rovers during the 90s, as well as for Galway United, Finn Harps and Newry Town. With the Bit O'Red he won an FAI Cup and found the net against Club Brugge in the old Cup Winners Cup. And then in 1995, Kenny was one of two home-based players, the other being Shamrock Rovers' John Toal, who were asked to train with Ireland squad under Jack Charlton, in advance of the friendly with England. A chance to see the pros up front for a player who never went full-time. Kenny was present in the ground as the English started their own demolition job on a ground that was creaking.
stories.rssSummary: Shamrock Gaels secretary Paul Brennan on the strong family links that have permeated successful times for the club, with their defence of the Sligo SFC title to come against St Mary's.

stories.title: Meyler: 'Surprised' to see Horan as integration chair
stories.summary: Former Tyrone footballer Conor Meyler has admitted that he was surprised to see former GAA president John Horan named as the new chair of the Steering Group on Integration. The Dubliner was appointed earlier in the week, following the resignation of Dr Mary McAleese from the position. "I'm probably surprised that they went with someone who has a background in the GAA. I know I've been quite vocal before about my own personal opinion and what research steered me, and my supervisory team, towards within the PhD. "That was having an independent chair was the best move, going with something more competency-based, somebody who's come through a process that's been similar in terms of sporting governance, gender reform and merger process. "So I was surprised, (but) I don't know John personally and I have no doubt that he will do a great job. He has obviously come in as well. "This isn't just a GAA decision. The LGFA and Camogie (Association) are obviously all agreed on the decision, which is interesting as well.

stories.title: Connacht mauled by ruthless Glasgow set-piece
stories.summary: Glasgow Warriors scored four maul tries as they defeated Connacht 36-19 in Scotstoun in round three of the United Rugby Championship. The visitors took the lead early on courtesy of Ireland international Sean Jansen as he burrowed over after just 14 minutes, but it was one way traffic for the rest of the half. First Glasgow hooker Gregor Hiddleston dotted down for the first maul try, before Rory Darge put the hosts in the lead shortly after the half hour mark. In a patient first half, where a greasy ball hampered any real chance of game-breaking rugby, the next score would come on the stroke of the interval. With Sam Illo sinbinned for a maul infringement, the Scottish club went back into the corner and powered over, with Hiddleston getting his second try of the night to give Glasgow a 19-7 half-time lead. It got worse for Connacht just moments into the second half as the hosts nabbed a try bonus point. Dan Lancaster's perfectly weighted cross-field kick was gathered by Jamie Dobie who grubber kicked behind Mack Hansen, with Josh McKay racing in to score.

stories.title: Something for the Weekend: Elizabeth Magill's cultural picks
stories.summary: Northern Sky is an exhibition of new paintings by artist Elizabeth Magill at Dublin's Kerlin Gallery. Magill is one of the Kerlin's longest-standing artist collaborations, established when the gallery first opened in 1988. Since then, she has enjoyed a celebrated international career, exhibiting in multiple public and commercial galleries across UK, Europe and Asia. Of the paintings in Northern Sky, novelist Colm Tóibín writes: "The drama is these paintings is released and withheld. Sometimes there is wind; sometimes there is stillness. What is plain sits uneasily beside what is visionary. There is no simple meaning; instead, there is much ambiguity and strange, coiled beauty. Something might be about to happen, but that possibility is contained. It is as though the landscape is holding its breath and releasing its breath." A recent film I liked was called Blue Heron by a Canadian director called Sophy Romvari about her dysfunctional brother and how that impacted the whole family. Recently on Netflix, I watched a couple of good films: Harvest, an adaptation of a book by Jim Crace and another one called First They Killed My Father about the war in Cambodia from a child's perspective. The title of my current exhibition at the Kerlin Gallery came from a song written and performed by the late Nick Drake. I chose it because of his beautiful lyrics and voice, but also with my paintings I was trying to convey the stark luminosity you sometimes experience from skies in a northern hemisphere. My previous show was called By This River, from a Brian Eno song whereby all my painting were from his lyrics. But I’m drawn to many different types of music… too many to mention. I just finished, Chloe Iridjis' The Shadow of the Object, and I’m reading London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe, both very different books. Irdjis’ novel is nuanced and quietly powerful and Radden Keefe is fast-paced and based on a true family tragedy alongside the ever flowing river Thames and the distortions created by excessive wealth in the 80’s and 90’s London.

stories.title: Dermot Kennedy to reschedule US gigs over voice damage
stories.summary: Dermot Kennedy has announced the rescheduling of the rest of his US tour to avoid suffering "long-lasting damage" to his vocal cords. The singer-songwriter, 34, had been due to play in Atlanta, Georgia. However, in a statement on Instagram he said he needed to postpone the remainder of his shows after an infection left his vocal cords "very swollen". He wrote: "Hey guys, I went to see another specialist in Atlanta today, and turns out the laryngitis still isn't gone, and because of the infection my vocal cords are still very swollen. "It’s frustrating, because I’ve been on vocal rest all week, which I thought would do enough, but apparently it hasn’t. "I can’t sing right now, and I wouldn’t be able to make it through a show, and if I did force myself to carry on without healing fully, I’d just end up doing real long-lasting damage.

stories.title: Irish designer Sasha Donnellan on finding her calling in Paris
stories.summary: Ellen Corcoran meets with Sasha Donnellan, the Irish designer who has captivated celebrity clients like Laura Whitmore and Roz Purcell, ahead of a dazzling presentation of her work during Paris Fashion Week. In the foyer of Hôtel Le Marois, I meet an elated and energetic Sasha Donnellan. She has a suitcase full of garments to bring back to Ireland ahead of her Ireland Fashion Week show in Dublin on Sunday morning, where she will showcase her full 20-look collection. The crowd finally fizzles out of the building and we find a seat by a grand piano as she catches her breath. Just 15 minutes earlier, a glimpse of her brand new collection, 'The Calling', had graced the runway for the very first time as part of Flying Solo NYC’s Paris Fashion Week show. Naturally, I ask how she’s feeling. "I was very nervous, of course, but also excited to see how people would perceive it, because I think this collection is quite different to my previous work", she says. "I feel like previous collections were much more focused on silks, and this time, I really leaned into my outerwear interest. That's something I haven't done before. So I was excited to see how people would react." Sasha refers to each of her collections as "little chapters" of her life. "I’m a designer, I love storytelling. To me, each collection represents a chapter that reflects something I'm incredibly passionate about at that moment." This time, that meant exploring the idea of a calling. Following her hugely successful Ireland Fashion Week debut in 2025, Sasha made the decision to become independent and commit fully to working on her brand, a move that prompted her to think about the people throughout history who had followed their own sense of purpose.

stories.summary: US President Donald Trump said that his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin would like to reach a deal on the war with Ukraine, accusing leader Volodymyr Zelensky of resisting a compromise. "Russia would like to make a deal... but for whatever reason, Zelensky does not want to make a deal," Mr Trump told reporters. "President Putin would like to see a settlement, strongly," Mr Trump said of what the Russian leader told him on Friday when the pair spoke on the phone. Mr Trump criticised the Ukrainian president for not holding an election since Russia first invaded Ukraine in 2022. "I think he should have an election and he could have settled this thing many times," Mr Trump said. Mr Trump and Mr Zelensky traded barbs yesterday after the US moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.

stories.title: Tech union to hold AI 'counter summit'
stories.summary: The Communications Workers' Union (CWU), which represents tech workers, is to hold an AI 'counter summit' to highlight the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs. It comes ahead of the International AI Summit which takes place in Dublin on Wednesday as part of Ireland's EU Presidency. The CWU said the event will present a "real world" analysis of the impact of AI on workers and highlight opposition to the adoption of new technologies without consultation with staff. The event is organised by the Digital and Tech Workers Alliance branch of the CWU. "The idea that AI should be developed and deployed simply for profit, regardless of its impact on workers and communities is dangerous," said CWU Deputy General Secretary Ian McArdle. "We need to reject tech products that oppose our social interests and big tech’s desire to achieve AI profitability at all costs."

stories.title: Irish officials say deal reached on EU savings union
stories.summary: Irish officials say a deal has been reached between EU finance ministers on a key element of the proposed Savings and Investment Union (SIU), a set of new rules designed to enhance cross-border investing in order to boost Europe's competitiveness. Officials say it is the most significant "win" of the Irish Presidency of the Council of the EU so far. Tánaiste Simon Harris has hailed the agreement as "a practical step towards a more integrated, competitive and resilient European economy". The agreement was hammered out at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Luxembourg this morning, chaired by Mr Harris. Ministers accepted a compromise text on how deeper cross-border integration in financial services will be supervised at EU level. The SIU is a key element of the push to lower barriers to cross-border financial services, in order to deepen a pool of capital that can boost Europe's competitiveness and fund more scale-up champions.

stories.title: €1 billion initiative to help businesses scale globally
stories.summary: A new €1 billion investment initiative which aims to help create the next generation of Irish companies of scale has been launched. The new fund will be administered by the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) - part of the National Treasury Management Agency - and will run until 2030. The initiative aims to ensure ambitious businesses here have access to capital to grow internationally while maintaining a significant presence in Ireland. It will focus on sectors where Ireland has potential to build globally competitive businesses, including the tech, life sciences, business services, food and other sectors. ISIF has already backed over 500 Irish companies under its Scaling Businesses investment theme, and this initiative expands and accelerates that strategy. Recent direct investments in businesses include Proverum (medical devices), Equal1 (quantum computing), Progress Systems (financial services software) and Cameramatics (fleet management).

stories.title: Cullen wants to more from Leinster after 'disjointed' win
stories.summary: Leinster head coach Leo Cullen wasn't getting carried away by his side's 29-5 win against Cardiff at Laya Arena, insisting the province will have to get better after what he described as a "disjointed" performance. The defending URC champions marked their first game at the newly redeveloped RDS by scoring five tries to one against the Welsh side, as they held Cardiff at arm’s length to register their first win of the season, in front of a near sold out crowd of 20,035 people. At half time, it looked like Leinster were set to pull away from Corniel van Zyl’s side, leading 22-5 with a bonus-point already secure. However, a sloppy third quarter meant they spent much of the second half defending, before a late Jamie Osborne try killed things off. "Up and running" was how Cullen summed things up after the 24-point victory, but while he was pleased to pick up a first win of the season - with nine of the starting team making their first appearances of the season - he was far from delighted. "Lots of good stuff in the first half. Unfortunately, at the start of the second half we don't put on much of a show, it gets a bit disjointed.

stories.title: Sibling rivalry: Franklin brothers battle for Down crown
stories.summary: They say nothing is guaranteed in championship football but this weekend's Down Intermediate Football Champions final between An Ríocht and Rostrevor is set to buck the trend. Whatever transpires in Newry – and barring a replay, of course – a Franklin brother will manage his side to victory. Tom Franklin is in charge of Rostrevor, his older brother Kevin is manager of An Ríocht alongside Paul Shields. It’s perhaps even a first in the GAA world. Siblings have come up against each other on the pitch, coaches have even had to manage against their own club on occasion, but a set of managerial brothers facing off in their biggest game of the year? Now that’s different. Rather than adding tension, the pair, who have coached alongside each other for the majority of their careers, have been looking at it as a light-hearted coincidence that simply adds to the whole razzamatazz that engulfs clubs in the lead-up to a county final. It has consumed their family too but for Tom there’s no doubting who their mother Rita will be lending 55% of her support to.

stories.title: Championship wrap: Idah heads Swans to victory
stories.summary: Adam Idah made up for three near misses in the first half to head Championship leaders Swansea to a 2-1 home win over Norwich. The Republic of Ireland striker came back to haunt his first club with a glancing header in the 59th minute to complete his side's comeback after falling behind to Jacob Wright’s goal in the first half. Joseph Opoku gave top scorer Idah a great chance to add to his three goals already this season in the 22nd minute after winning the ball on halfway and driving to the Norwich box. Idah took a heavy touch from what looked to be a scoring pass and Kovacevic saved. Norwich were quick on the counter-attack and a great cross from the left forced Stephen Welsh to head over from under the Swansea bar to concede a corner. The corner was cleared but Andre Brooks and Oscar Schwartau combined to rob Welsh of the ball and Schwartau passed across the box to enable Wright to score in the 28th minute. Idah had two more chances to level matters before the break, but again Kovacevic was up to the mark to deny him.

stories.title: New Zealand make light work of Aussies in Auckland
stories.summary: Australia's hopes of wresting back the Bledisloe Cup for the first time in a generation were crushed in familiar fashion in a comprehensive 50-19 loss to New Zealand at Auckland's Eden Park. The Wallabies were ⁠in touch at 17-14 down at half-time but the All Blacks scored five tries after the break to ensure they will retain the symbol of trans-Tasman Sea supremacy for a 24th straight year ahead of next week's second test in Sydney. Tries from Peter Lakai, Tupou Vaa'i, Cam Roigard, skipper Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby and Will Jordan combined with 15 points from the boot of fly-half Damian McKenzie got the All Blacks back to winning ways after three straight losses to South Africa. Australia, who came into the game unbeaten in six matches and looking for a first win at Eden Park since 1986, scored first-half tries through fullback Tom ‌Wright and captain Harry Wilson and earned ⁠a late consolation score from hooker Josh Nasser. The Wallabies, buoyed by a win over world champions South Africa last month, dominated the opening exchanges and got their reward in the eighth minute when fullback Wright cleverly straightened up an attacking move to score the opening try. The aerial battle was always going to be a key factor and New Zealand were enjoying the better of it with Jordie Barrett winning ‌one duel and feeding McKenzie, who scythed through the defence before feeding flanker Lakai to level up the scores.

stories.title: Dream big - inside The Ark's new anthology of plays for kids
stories.summary: Aideen Howard, creative director of The Ark, introduces Dream Big, the new book collecting a quintet of original (and acclaimed) theatre works commissioned by the children's cultural centre. As a young drama student in 1995, I remember vividly the excitement surrounding the opening of Europe's first ever dedicated children cultural centre. That this ground-breaking innovation was happening in the heart of Dublin city was a source of pride. The Ark Children’s Cultural Centre opened its doors in Temple Bar, three years after the Irish government ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of The Child which recognised the right of children to 'participate freely in cultural life and the arts.’ History was being made. Ireland was showing a new cultural confidence in its vision for investment in both the arts and children. Now, thirty years after its founding, over a million children and their parents and teachers have attended The Ark. Our purpose is to realise children’s right to art and culture with ambition and joy. We do so by commissioning, producing and presenting new art for, by, with and about children from birth to age 12. From the beginning I was inspired by The Ark’s radical approach to art making and community engagement. When I was appointed Director in 2015, I was keen to build on those strong foundations. One of my first projects was to introduce a child participation practice to redistribute decision making power across the organisation alongside a new commissioning strategy. The Ark Children’s Council was established and now plays a key role in all decision-making and inform the development of every new commission. The five writers featured in Dream Big have created new worlds of the imagination.

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (October 9-11)
stories.summary: From a swap shop in Tallaght to a harvest fair in Naul, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. Ready to change up your wardrobe for winter? Swap Til Ye Drop is hosting a sustainably-minded day of shopping at Red Rua in Tallaght on Friday, 9 October, from 5pm-9pm. Bring along up to 10 items of clothes, shoes, accessories and/or books to swap (clean and in good condition). Then you're free to go swapping from what everyone else has brought. Additionally, there will be a repair/upcycling cafe available, so bring along an item or two that needs some TLC. The cast of Pretty Good Improv (Luke Benson, Stephen Bradley, Avril Burke, Niall Johnson, Ross McCarney, Kate Moylan, John Spillane) are teaming up with the cast of Failed State (John Purcell, Malin von Euler-Hogan, and special guest Kelley Quinn of UBC NY) to deliver an unforgettable night of comedy. The show will take place at The Pearse Centre on Friday, 9 October, at 8pm. Tickets €7. Alternative Dublin is hosting a series of spooky social events this October as part of the Dublin Halloween Festival. Their beginner-friendly night of crochet will take place at This Must Be The Place on Saturday, 10 October, at 3pm. You’ll learn how to get comfortable with a crochet hook and yarn, practise basic crochet techniques, and create a handmade pumpkin. All materials are provided. Tickets are €25.64. PIERCED on Camden Street is launching their new Claddagh collection with drinks, snacks, bedazzling, photo ops, discounts & prizes. Taking place on Friday, 9 October, from 5pm-9pm, there will even be a bedazzling station where you can decorate your own Claddagh keyring to take home. €15 ticket, fully redeemable in store on the night. Now in its 21st year, Maths Week runs from Saturday 10th to Saturday 18th October, with events taking place in schools, universities, libraries, visitor centres, parks and even on city streets. Family-friendly events include free outdoor maths trails where children and adults can find and solve puzzles in local parks, as well as exhibits, activities, and more. See the full programme here.

stories.title: New investment account: greater returns or greater risks?
stories.summary: The new State-backed investment account has been hailed as the first serious attempt to make investment more appealing to the Irish public. Irish consumers are among Europe's best savers, but lag when it comes to putting their money to work, according to the Central Bank. Its figures show households here hold only about 2.3% of their financial assets directly in listed shares and debt securities, compared with an EU average of 7.5%. According to the details announced by Minister for Finance Simon Harris, there will be no minimum contribution, so savers can start with even the smallest amount. Money in the account is tax-free up to €50,000. Above that, a 1% annual charge applies to the value above the threshold (not just to returns). Savers will be able to invest in shares, bonds, and ETFs, while complex and risky products, including derivatives and crypto assets, will not be eligible.

stories.title: HSE urges people reach out on World Mental Health Day
stories.summary: The HSE is encouraging people to reach out for support "if they are finding things difficult", as it marks World Mental Health Day. So far this year around 6,000 people have availed of the HSE's free online therapy service. Over 40,000 people have accessed the Cognitive Behavioural Therapy programmes since the service was launched in 2021. "Looking after our mental health is something we can all do, just as we look after our physical health," advises Brian Higgins, HSE Assistant National Director of Adult Mental Health. "We want people to know that there are many free supports available right now and that you do not have to face things alone." He said a conversation, a phone call or simply letting someone know how and where they can get help could make an important difference.

stories.title: Polanski vows to stay Greens leader despite election loss
stories.summary: Zack Polanski has insisted he will carry on as Greens leader despite failing to win a seat in Parliament as the fallout continued from the party conference backing a motion declaring Zionism is racism. The UK Green Party leader's position was being questioned by senior colleagues even before he was unsuccessful in ousting Labour in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election triggered by the resignation of former prime minister Keir Starmer. Mr Polanski said "of course I can carry on" as party leader but acknowledged that ultimately Green members would decide his fate. He was defeated by Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali, who retained the north London seat for Labour. She secured 45% of the vote to the Greens' 33%, a majority of 3,364 but seeing a 13% swing to the Greens, whose vote share was up by 22.4%. Mr Polanski missed the Green Party conference vote which endorsed a policy effectively calling for Israel to be abolished and replaced with a single Palestinian state.

stories.title: Residents protest against major data centre in Waterford
stories.summary: Over 300 protesters have taken part in a slow drive protest in Kilmeaden, Co Waterford against a major data centre and energy development proposed near the village. A convoy of cars, tractors, vans and other vehicles set off from Ballyduff National School this morning. The convoy travelled through Kilmeaden by way of Kildermody towards the Kingsmeadow Roundabout on the Cork Road, before returning through the village. Crag Rathnew DC Limited and Kent Homes Limited are seeking permission to develop the former Kilmeaden cheese factory site and its adjoining lands. The planning application states that the proposed development would "provide for a mixed use village centre, technology park, and renewable energy development on a total site area of 108.79 hectares." Those behind the project have said that all of their facilities are designed and developed in line with regulatory guidelines and in consultation with community representatives.

stories.summary: A strong 7.6 magnitude earthquake struck near the southern coast of Panama at a 10km depth, according to the US Geological Survey. There were no immediate reports of damage in Panama, while television footage showed people evacuating buildings. The earthquake was downgraded from an earlier estimate of 8.0 magnitude. Tremors were felt in Panama City, where buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets. Visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the earthquake's impact. "We felt it very strongly," said one resident from the Herrera province, where the earthquake struck.

stories.summary: Derry City's interim boss Mark Connolly hailed the character of his players as they marched into the Club Orange FAI Cup final after a "whirlwind few months". Michael Duffy's brace earned the Candystripes a deserved 2-0 win at Galway United to set up an Aviva Stadium showdown with Waterford on Sunday 8 November. Connolly took the reins back in August after Tiernan Lynch departed. He's had to deal with a significant fallout between star man James McClean and the club, while stabilising Derry's erratic form. They're fifth, two points behind fourth-placed Shelbourne with four games to play. "I just think there's been a lot of expectation from the start of the season. They didn't reach that and they could have gone under a wee bit, even when the last manager left and I came in. "I'm just so proud of their effort and their desire... just super boys, so delighted.
